about: Every source of the mechanism timeline's record (docs/research/phase-5/mechanism.json), each fetched and read on the retrieval date. No source has a copy here: each was read and is not kept, and `fetchedSha256` is the sha256 of the file as it was fetched that day, a record of which file was read that nothing checks. Each `supports` row names in `fields` the stored values it supports, each by its place in the record with the item's id in brackets (thermo.formation[water].enthalpy, chapters[decomposition].timescale), and gives what the source prints for them and where. The tables of Wagman and others are the scan the aqueous reactions lab cites, under the same id and citation; that citation names the two pages that lab read, and the pages read for this record are named in the rows here. The library records and the ionic radii the timeline draws from are cited where they are stored, in src/chem-data. README.md says what was read as a check and is not cited, and what could not be sourced.

sources.citation: Pines, D.; Ditkovich, J.; Mukra, T.; Miller, Y.; Kiefer, P. M.; Daschakraborty, S.; Hynes, J. T.; Pines, E. How Acidic Is Carbonic Acid? J. Phys. Chem. B 2016, 120, 2440-2451. (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.5b12428) Read as the authors' manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5747581), linked here, fetched as XML through the National Center for Biotechnology Information's E-utilities, which carries the text, the tables and the captions of the figures but not the figures; the text read in full and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-07).

supports.where: The abstract, the end of section 5.2 and section 6: the acid constant of the carbonic acid molecule itself, given as a pKa with an uncertainty of 0.05. Section 5.2 gets it as the pKa of lactic acid, 3.86, less 0.37. It was not measured by titration: the rate at which an acid made by a flash of light hands a proton to hydrogen carbonate, lactate and pyruvate was timed by the fading of its fluorescence, and the pKa read from how that rate goes with acid strength. Section 3.1 gives the temperature of every experiment as 20.5 °C, give or take one degree, in ordinary water.

Section 1, second paragraph: carbonic acid in water breaks up into carbon dioxide and water with a lifetime the paper gives as about this many milliseconds at room temperature. The paper did not measure it: the sentence cites three earlier studies (of 1940, 1941 and 1963), which were not read.

Section 5.1, last paragraph: the rate constant, within a pair already in contact, of the proton's move to hydrogen carbonate. The proton comes from the light-made acid of the experiment, not from a hydronium ion. Its reciprocal is 18 picoseconds. Sections 3.2 and 4.1 time the whole process, which includes the two finding each other, on a scale of nanoseconds: a counting card of 5 ns or 50 ns full scale, and decays of about a nanosecond.
